title: New giant waterlily species described after chance Instagram sighting – and it’s already Critically Endangered

text:
New giant waterlily species described after chance Instagram sighting – and it’s already Critically Endangered
RELEASE DATE: 9 OCTOBER 2026

A new paper published today in the journal Phytotaxa unveils a new species in the genus Victoria, the Colombian giant waterlily (Victoria colombiana). With only three other known species in the genus, V. colombiana joins the pantheon of nature’s giants with pads measuring up to 2 metres across.

Carlos Magdalena, Botanical and Scientific Research Horticulturist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew was first made aware of the waterlily on Instagram five years ago when he spotted it in photos taken in Colombia's Inírida region by Jeremiah Harris. Harris, who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware at the time of the significance of his snapshot, mistakenly identifying the new species for the more common V. amazonica.

However, Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert, immediately suspected something wasn’t quite right as the natural range of known Victoria waterlilies does not extend to the Inírida River, in Guainía, Colombia, which is in the head water drainage of the Orinoco River, South America's third longest river and one of its most important waterways. This prompted him to speculate it could be a new species.

Once the team was ready, they set off into Inírida’s rainforest on a five-day expedition, yet by the fifth day it seemed they would return empty handed. They initially located just two individuals of the waterlily, but the plants were not in flower.

This was problematic as a fertile herbarium voucher – a pressed and dried plant specimen that crucially requires a flower – is critical for botanists to distinguish the differences between species, by comparing them to other herbarium vouchers, such as the 6.4 million stored at Kew's Herbarium. Furthermore, the plants they encountered appeared to be struggling with high-level waters and the late but intense rainy season.

With only 10 hours left to make their return flight, they set off at 1am in pitch-black darkness, heading in the opposite direction of the airport deeper and deeper into the flooded rainforest, trusting Melo’s skills and instinct to navigate through the tricky environment. Just before sunrise, the team reached a small lake in the middle of the jungle where they located a second population with five additional individuals of V. colombiana, including one that was in flower.

The discovery provided the material needed to begin the formal scientific description of the species, with the team documenting a total of seven plants across two lakes before miraculously rushing back to the airport just in time for their flight.

Subsequent analysis using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) done by Carlos A. Pedraza-Penalosa, from DreamGIS Colombia, revealed a third lake where the waterlily was present. Comparing satellite imagery suggested additional plants may become visible during the drier seasons when water levels drop. This, however, makes reaching the plants trickier as the terrain is easier to navigate by boat in the high season when the forests are flooded, than it is on foot.

At present, the team estimates there are between 30 and 50 individual V. colombiana plants in the wild, indicating the species is extremely rare and at threat of extinction. Searching for new unknown populations through more robust satellite imagery scanning to uncover the real number of individuals and natural populations is therefore essential, and the team are working towards an official IUCN Red List assessment of Critically Endangered.

There is hope however, as efforts are underway to support the long-term conservation of V. colombiana, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within Indigenous territory. Such a site could support local eco-tourism while providing an additional safeguarded population outside the species' remote natural habitat.

Researchers hope to continue efforts to collect seed, with the aim of cultivating plants in Bogotá and learning more about the species under controlled conditions. If the efforts are successful, it may even be grown one day at Kew Gardens alongside its cousins: V. amazonica, V. cruziana and V. boliviana.
